items.title: Architecture catalogue
items.summary: Generated canonical architecture index.

items.title: Availability
items.summary: The proportion of time a system is able to serve valid requests, usually expressed as a percentage of uptime measured at the service level indicator.
items.definition: The proportion of time a system is able to serve valid requests, usually expressed as a percentage of uptime measured at the service level indicator.
stimulus: A dependency degrades, a host fails, or traffic suddenly spikes beyond the normal peak.
A new release is deployed to production.
response: The system continues to answer valid requests, possibly in a degraded mode, and rejects excess load cleanly.
Failures are detected through symptom-based alerts and the blast radius stays confined.
measure: Monthly successful request ratio at or above 99.95 percent.
p95 request latency at or below 300 ms during normal operation.
Mean time to detect a user-visible failure under 5 minutes.
No single dependency fault reduces successful requests below 99 percent for more than 10 minutes.
use_when: A dependency degrades, a host fails, or traffic suddenly spikes beyond the normal peak.
A new release is deployed to production.

items.title: Modifiability
items.summary: The ease with which a system can be changed to add a feature, replace a component, or adapt to a new requirement without unintended effects elsewhere.
items.definition: The ease with which a system can be changed to add a feature, replace a component, or adapt to a new requirement without unintended effects elsewhere.
stimulus: A requirement changes, a datastore is swapped, a new read view is requested, or a library is upgraded.
response: The change is contained in one module or service, verified quickly, and released without a coordinated multi-team deployment.
measure: Change lead time under one working day for a localized feature.
At least 90 percent of changes require no cross-team coordination.
Time to add a new read projection under two days.
Replacement of a persistence adapter touches one layer and no domain files.
use_when: A requirement changes, a datastore is swapped, a new read view is requested, or a library is upgraded.

items.title: Performance
items.summary: The responsiveness and throughput of a system under a specified workload, commonly expressed as latency percentiles and requests handled per unit of time.
items.definition: The responsiveness and throughput of a system under a specified workload, commonly expressed as latency percentiles and requests handled per unit of time.
stimulus: A burst of concurrent requests, a large stream of records, or a peak traffic window arrives.
response: The system processes the load within its latency budget without unbounded queueing or resource exhaustion.
measure: p95 request latency at or below 300 ms and p99 at or below 1000 ms.
Sustained throughput of at least 5000 requests per second.
Cache hit ratio above 80 percent for read-heavy endpoints.
Backlog drains within 5 minutes after a traffic burst ends.
use_when: A burst of concurrent requests, a large stream of records, or a peak traffic window arrives.

items.title: Recoverability
items.summary: The ability of a system to restore an acceptable state and resume service after a failure, measured by how quickly and completely normal operation returns.
items.definition: The ability of a system to restore an acceptable state and resume service after a failure, measured by how quickly and completely normal operation returns.
stimulus: A service crashes, a region is lost, a bad release ships, or a batch of messages is processed incorrectly.
response: The system restores state from durable records or undoes partial work, resumes traffic automatically, and stays within the stated recovery targets.
measure: Recovery time objective of 30 minutes or less for a full service outage.
Recovery point objective of 5 minutes or less for durable data.
Rollback of a bad release completed in 60 seconds or less.
Event replay rebuilds projections within 15 minutes of a failure.
use_when: A service crashes, a region is lost, a bad release ships, or a batch of messages is processed incorrectly.

items.title: Security
items.summary: The ability of a system to protect data and resources from unauthorized access and misuse while remaining usable for legitimate requests.
items.definition: The ability of a system to protect data and resources from unauthorized access and misuse while remaining usable for legitimate requests.
stimulus: An unauthenticated caller, a hostile tenant, a leaked credential, or an attempt to flood shared capacity occurs.
response: Requests are authenticated and authorized, sensitive fields are protected, abusive capacity use is capped, and telemetry supports audit without exposing secrets.
measure: 100 percent of external endpoints enforce authentication and authorization.
Zero critical or high findings in dependency and configuration scans.
Zero recorded secret or personal data leaks in application logs over each audit period.
Compromised credential revoked in 5 minutes or less.
Audit logs retained for 365 days.
use_when: An unauthenticated caller, a hostile tenant, a leaked credential, or an attempt to flood shared capacity occurs.

items.title: Testability
items.summary: The ease with which a system can be verified against its specification by isolating parts, controlling their inputs, and observing their outputs.
items.definition: The ease with which a system can be verified against its specification by isolating parts, controlling their inputs, and observing their outputs.
stimulus: A new feature is added, a fault must be injected, or a regression suite runs before a release.
response: Components can be exercised independently with deterministic inputs and observable outputs, and failure paths can be reproduced on demand.
measure: Unit test runtime under 60 seconds for a single service.
Full integration suite runtime under 10 minutes.
At least 90 percent of critical paths covered by failure-injection cases.
Every filter or handler testable with fixture input and no live broker.
use_when: A new feature is added, a fault must be injected, or a regression suite runs before a release.

items.title: Command Query Responsibility Segregation
items.summary: Use separate models to update state and to read state, so each side can be optimized, scaled, and evolved for its own workload.
items.decision: Route writes through a command model and maintain one or more read projections from the resulting events, accepting replication lag in return for independent read and write design.
use_when: Read and write workloads have very different volume or shape.
Complex queries would distort the write model.
Several read views of the same data are needed.
avoid_when: Read-after-write consistency must be immediate for every user action.
The domain is simple and one model already serves both paths well.
The team cannot maintain projection rebuild and lag monitoring.

tradeoffs.benefit: Read views can be denormalized for fast queries without constraining writes.
tradeoffs.cost: Replication lag means a just-written value may be absent from a read view.

tradeoffs.benefit: Read and write sides scale and deploy independently.
tradeoffs.cost: Projections must be rebuilt on schema change, which costs time and operational care.

quality_impacts.note: Purpose-built read views reduce query fan-out and can hold p95 latency flat as read volume grows.
Read models can be added without touching commands, shortening change lead time for new views.
Projections can be rebuilt from the event log within a stated RTO after corruption or loss.

components.name: Command model
components.role: Validates and applies business rules to state changes and emits resulting events.

components.name: Event log
components.role: Records accepted state changes as the durable source of truth for projections.

components.name: Projection builder
components.role: Consumes events and updates read models, tracking progress for replay and recovery.

components.name: Query model
components.role: Serves reads from purpose-built, denormalized views tuned for specific queries.

items.title: Event-Driven Architecture
items.summary: Components produce and consume immutable domain events so services react to facts that already happened without a synchronous caller waiting for the result.
items.decision: Publish facts to a durable broker and let subscribers evolve independently, accepting eventual consistency in exchange for loose coupling and burst absorption.
use_when: Several downstream services must react to the same business fact.
Work arrives in bursts and producers should not block on consumers.
Audit trails and replay of past facts are valuable.
avoid_when: The workflow needs one strongly consistent transaction across services.
The team cannot operate a broker and watch consumer lag.
Simple synchronous request-response reads dominate the workload.

tradeoffs.benefit: Producers and consumers can be deployed and scaled independently.
tradeoffs.cost: Eventual consistency forces the UI to handle stale reads and pending state.

tradeoffs.benefit: A durable log allows replay and new subscribers without backfilling live systems.
tradeoffs.cost: Duplicate delivery requires idempotent handlers and careful ordering design.

quality_impacts.note: A slow or down consumer does not fail the producer, so the ingress path stays available during bursts.
Adding a subscriber is a local change that does not edit the producer, shortening change lead time.
Replaying the log rebuilds projections after a failure, supporting a defined RTO without manual data repair.

components.name: Producer
components.role: Detects a state change and publishes an immutable event describing the fact.

components.name: Event broker
components.role: Durably stores and routes events to subscribers with at-least-once delivery.

components.name: Consumer
components.role: Subscribes to event types, applies idempotent state changes, and emits follow-up events.

components.name: Event log
components.role: Retains the ordered fact history for replay, auditing, and projection rebuilding.

items.title: Layered Architecture
items.summary: Organize code into horizontal layers where each layer depends only on the layer directly beneath it, separating presentation, application, domain, and persistence concerns.
items.decision: Split the system into presentation, application, domain, and infrastructure layers and enforce one-way dependencies so a storage change does not ripple into business rules.
use_when: The domain is stable and the user interface or data store is likely to change.
A team wants a low-complexity default with clear separation of concerns.
Requirements map to CRUD screens over a relational model.
avoid_when: Read and write paths need independent scaling under very different load.
Deep synchronous call chains make latency budgets hard to meet.
Domain logic is thin and layering adds ceremony without benefit.

tradeoffs.benefit: Changes to a single concern stay local when dependencies point inward.
tradeoffs.cost: A request typically crosses every layer, adding indirection and call overhead.

tradeoffs.benefit: New developers find a familiar and easy-to-explain structure.
tradeoffs.cost: Rigid layering can encourage anemic domain models that only pass data through.

quality_impacts.note: Replacing a persistence adapter changes one layer and leaves domain rules untouched, cutting change lead time.
Domain and application layers can be tested without a database or UI, keeping unit test runtime under one minute.
Synchronous traversal of four layers adds hops that can raise p95 latency on read-heavy endpoints.

components.name: Presentation
components.role: Renders user-facing screens or public HTTP responses and translates input into application calls.

components.name: Application
components.role: Coordinates use cases and orchestrates domain objects without holding business rules.

components.name: Domain
components.role: Holds entities, value objects, and business invariants independent of delivery and storage.

components.name: Infrastructure
components.role: Implements persistence, messaging, and external adapters behind interfaces defined by inner layers.

items.title: Microservices Architecture
items.summary: Decompose a system into small services aligned to business capabilities, each owning its data and exposing a network API so teams can deploy and scale independently.
items.decision: Draw service boundaries around bounded contexts with separate datastores, and accept distributed-systems complexity in exchange for independent release cadence and fault isolation.
use_when: Multiple teams need to release features on different schedules.
Subdomains have sharply different scaling or availability needs.
Clear bounded contexts with stable interfaces can be identified.
avoid_when: The product is early and domain boundaries are still uncertain.
The team lacks tooling for deployment, tracing, and incident response.
A single database transaction must span most operations.

tradeoffs.benefit: Teams can change and deploy their own service without a coordinated release.
tradeoffs.cost: Network calls replace in-process calls, adding latency and partial failure modes.

tradeoffs.benefit: A failure in one service can be isolated with bulkheads and breakers.
tradeoffs.cost: Distributed data requires sagas and eventual consistency instead of simple joins.

quality_impacts.note: A capability change is contained in one service, reducing change lead time from weeks to days.
Independent deployment and bulkheads limit the blast radius of a bad release to one service.
Chatty inter-service calls can lift p95 latency unless boundaries are coarse and caches are used.

components.name: Service
components.role: Owns one business capability, its data, and its own deployment lifecycle.

components.name: API gateway
components.role: Provides a single entry point for clients and handles routing, authentication, and rate limits.

components.name: Service datastore
components.role: Persists state private to one service so schemas cannot be coupled across teams.

components.name: Messaging backbone
components.role: Carries asynchronous events and commands between services without direct coupling.

items.title: Pipe and Filter
items.summary: Compose a stream of processing stages where each filter transforms data incrementally and passes results to the next stage through a buffer or pipe.
items.decision: Break a data workflow into small independent filters connected by bounded pipes so stages can be reused, reordered, and scaled without rewriting the whole pipeline.
use_when: Data can be processed incrementally as a stream.
Stages are reusable and can be recombined for different jobs.
Throughput matters more than single-record round-trip latency.
avoid_when: Each record needs a long interactive transaction across stages.
Stages must share large mutable state.
Strict end-to-end ordering with no buffering is required.

tradeoffs.benefit: Filters are small, reusable, and easy to test in isolation.
tradeoffs.cost: Serializing records between stages adds CPU and memory overhead.

tradeoffs.benefit: Slow stages can be scaled independently behind bounded buffers.
tradeoffs.cost: A failing stage can block or drop records unless dead-letter handling is designed in.

quality_impacts.note: Inserting or replacing one filter is a local change, shortening change lead time for new transformations.
Each filter can be verified with fixture input and output in isolation, keeping test runtime short.
Bounded pipes let stages run concurrently and absorb bursts, raising sustained throughput and steadying p95 latency.

components.name: Source
components.role: Emits raw records into the first pipe from a file, stream, or message topic.

components.name: Filter
components.role: Performs one focused transformation and emits output without knowing upstream or downstream stages.

components.name: Pipe
components.role: Buffers and transports records between filters, decoupling their processing rates.

components.name: Sink
components.role: Persists or forwards the final transformed records to their destination.

items.title: Serverless Architecture
items.summary: Run application logic in short-lived managed functions triggered by events, with the platform handling capacity, scaling, and operational plumbing.
items.decision: Express behaviour as small functions behind managed triggers and pay for actual execution, accepting cold starts and statelessness in exchange for minimal idle cost and elastic scale.
use_when: Traffic is spiky or unpredictable and idle capacity would be wasted.
Work is naturally event driven, such as API requests, queues, or schedules.
A small team wants to avoid server and runtime patching.
avoid_when: Workloads are long-running, CPU-bound, or need persistent in-process state.
Strict p95 latency budgets cannot tolerate cold starts.
Deep vendor-specific integration is unacceptable.

tradeoffs.benefit: Capacity scales to zero and back without provisioning servers.
tradeoffs.cost: Cold starts can add hundreds of milliseconds to p95 latency for infrequent paths.

tradeoffs.benefit: The team stops managing operating systems and runtime patching.
tradeoffs.cost: Stateless execution pushes all state to external services and complicates local testing.

quality_impacts.note: Horizontal scale follows demand automatically, keeping p95 latency stable under bursty load once functions are warm.
Managed triggers and multi-zone execution remove single-server failure points from the request path.
Small functions with narrow triggers allow feature changes to ship in minutes, shortening change lead time.

components.name: Function
components.role: Executes one stateless unit of business logic in response to a trigger.

components.name: API gateway
components.role: Maps HTTP requests to functions and handles throttling and request validation.

components.name: Managed trigger
components.role: Starts a function from a queue, schedule, object store, or stream event.

components.name: Managed datastore
components.role: Stores durable state outside the function so invocations remain stateless.

items.title: Blue-Green Deploy
items.summary: Run two identical production environments and switch traffic from the current one to the prepared one only after the new version is verified.
items.decision: Keep a stable blue environment serving users while green is deployed and tested, then flip the router or DNS so rollback is a fast switch back rather than a redeploy.
use_when: Rollback must be fast and predictable for availability targets.
The environment can be duplicated at acceptable cost.
Releases are infrequent enough that warm standby capacity is justified.
avoid_when: Infrastructure cost of a full second environment is unacceptable.
The system is stateful in a way that prevents quick traffic switching.
Deployments happen many times a day with tiny changes and rolling updates suffice.

tradeoffs.benefit: Rollback is a traffic switch, reducing recovery time after a bad release.
tradeoffs.cost: Doubling capacity for the standby environment raises cost.

tradeoffs.benefit: Green can be validated with real traffic patterns before users see it.
tradeoffs.cost: Database migrations must be backward compatible across both versions.

quality_impacts.note: Instant traffic switch and rollback protect the availability percentage during releases.
A bad release is undone within seconds, well inside the RTO for a failed deployment.
Isolated release environments let changes ship with less coordination, shortening change lead time.

items.mechanism: Provision an equal green environment, deploy and smoke-test the new release there, shift traffic gradually or atomically at the router, and keep blue warm for immediate rollback.
failure_modes: Shared state or schema changes that make one version incompatible with the other.
Cutting over before green passes health and smoke checks.
Draining blue too quickly so rollback is no longer instant.
Sticky sessions keeping users on the old version after the switch.

items.title: Bulkhead
items.summary: Partition capacity into isolated pools so a failure or traffic surge in one area cannot consume all resources and starve unrelated work.
items.decision: Allocate separate thread pools, connection pools, queues, or compute quotas per workload and cap each pool so one caller cannot exhaust the whole system.
use_when: Multiple tenants or workloads share one process or cluster.
A slow dependency must not block unrelated requests.
Blast radius must be bounded for availability targets.
avoid_when: The system has a single workload with uniform priority.
Resource overhead of many pools exceeds the available budget.
Work cannot be classified before resources are assigned.

tradeoffs.benefit: A stuck dependency is contained, keeping other request classes available.
tradeoffs.cost: Static partitions waste idle capacity that another pool could use.

tradeoffs.benefit: Bounded queues give predictable memory use and p95 latency under load.
tradeoffs.cost: Requests beyond a pool cap are rejected and need explicit fallback handling.

quality_impacts.note: Isolated pools keep critical paths serving traffic when a noncritical path saturates, protecting the availability percentage.
Bounded queues prevent unbounded waits and keep p95 latency predictable during bursts.
Per-tenant quotas limit how much capacity one noisy or hostile client can consume.

items.mechanism: Assign each dependency or request class its own bounded resource pool with a fixed size and queue, and reject or shed load locally when that pool is full.
failure_modes: Pools sized so generously that an overload still exhausts the shared host.
Too many small pools wasting capacity that could be shared.
Forgetting to isolate the connection pool while isolating threads.
No backpressure, so an unbounded queue grows until memory is exhausted.

items.title: Cache Aside
items.summary: Load data into a cache on demand from the application, reading from the cache first and populating it from the source of truth on a miss.
items.decision: Treat the datastore as authoritative and let application code populate the cache lazily with a time to live and invalidation on writes.
use_when: Reads greatly outnumber writes and data is reused.
Some staleness within a defined freshness window is acceptable.
The source datastore cannot sustain peak read load alone.
avoid_when: Every read must see the latest committed write.
Data is write-heavy or almost never reused.
The value is large relative to the cache and churns constantly.

tradeoffs.benefit: Common reads avoid a datastore round trip and lower p95 latency.
tradeoffs.cost: Invalidation logic adds application complexity and stale windows.

tradeoffs.benefit: Read load on the primary datastore drops, improving headroom and availability.
tradeoffs.cost: A cold cache produces a latency spike and a burst of datastore traffic.

quality_impacts.note: Serving hot keys from cache reduces p95 latency and datastore load during peak traffic.
Cached reads remain answerable during a short datastore outage within the freshness window.
Cache policy lives in application code and can be tuned without a datastore schema change, shortening change lead time.

items.mechanism: On read, check the cache, return a hit, or read the datastore, write the result to the cache with an expiry, then return it; on write, update the datastore and invalidate or refresh the cached key.
failure_modes: Stale reads when writes update the datastore but forget to invalidate the cache.
Cache stampede when many callers miss the same hot key at once.
Caching unbounded key variants that crowd out useful entries.
Treating the cache as the source of truth and losing data on eviction.

items.title: Circuit Breaker
items.summary: Stop sending requests to a failing dependency for a cooling-off period, then probe cautiously before restoring normal traffic.
items.decision: Wrap calls in a breaker that trips after a failure threshold, fails fast while open, and moves through half-open probes to decide when to close.
use_when: A remote dependency can degrade or fail for a sustained period.
Failing fast is better than queueing calls that will time out.
A fallback response or degraded mode exists.
avoid_when: The dependency is in-process with no independent failure mode.
No acceptable degraded response exists and every call must be attempted.
Call volume is so low that a failure threshold is rarely reached.

tradeoffs.benefit: Fast failure protects callers from p95 latency blowups and thread exhaustion.
tradeoffs.cost: Requests are rejected even after the dependency begins to recover until a probe succeeds.

tradeoffs.benefit: A failing dependency gets time to recover without sustained load.
tradeoffs.cost: Requires tuning thresholds, windows, and timeouts per dependency.

quality_impacts.note: Fail-fast behaviour keeps the caller available and preserves error budget when a downstream service degrades.
Half-open probes detect recovery and restore traffic automatically, shortening recovery time within the RTO.
Rejecting calls without waiting on timeouts holds p95 latency steady during a downstream outage.

items.mechanism: Count failures in a rolling window, open the circuit when the threshold is crossed, reject calls immediately while open, and allow a limited probe after a timeout.
failure_modes: Tripping on a slow but healthy dependency because timeouts are set too tightly.
Flapping when thresholds are too sensitive to brief noise.
Sharing one breaker across unrelated dependencies so one fault blocks all.
Treating business errors as dependency failures and opening incorrectly.

items.title: Idempotent Consumer
items.summary: Make message handling safe to repeat so redelivery of the same event produces exactly the same observable result as a single delivery.
items.decision: Attach a stable identity to each message and record processed identities atomically with the resulting state change so duplicates are detected and skipped.
use_when: A broker delivers at least once and duplicates are expected.
Retry and replay are part of normal operation.
Side effects can be tied to a stable message identity.
avoid_when: Delivery is genuinely exactly once and never replayed.
The operation has no persistent state to record keys.
Each identical request is meant to produce a distinct effect.

tradeoffs.benefit: Retries and replay become safe, improving recoverability after failures.
tradeoffs.cost: A deduplication store adds a read or unique constraint on every message.

tradeoffs.benefit: Duplicate events no longer corrupt counts or create repeated orders.
tradeoffs.cost: Key retention must be designed so old duplicates cannot be accepted after cleanup.

quality_impacts.note: Replaying a log after a crash is safe because repeated events are skipped, supporting the RTO and RPO targets.
Consumers can acknowledge and retry freely without manual cleanup, keeping the pipeline available during faults.
Deduplication lookups add a datastore operation per message, raising p95 latency for high-volume consumers.

items.mechanism: Extract a deduplication key, check a processed-key store or unique constraint inside the same transaction as the side effect, commit once, and treat a duplicate as a successful no-op.
failure_modes: Recording the key separately from the state change so a crash leaves them inconsistent.
Using a key that changes on redelivery and defeats detection.
Keeping deduplication records forever without a retention policy.
Assuming exactly-once delivery from a broker that provides at-least-once.

items.title: Observability
items.summary: Instrument the system so its internal state can be inferred from externally emitted logs, metrics, and traces without shipping new code during an incident.
items.decision: Emit structured telemetry with correlation identifiers across every service boundary, define service level indicators up front, and build dashboards and alerts around user-visible symptoms.
use_when: The system is distributed and failures cross service boundaries.
Availability and latency targets must be measured, not guessed.
On-call responders need fast triage with runbooks.
avoid_when: The system is a single process with trivial behaviour and short lifetime.
There is no capacity to store or respond to telemetry.
Telemetry would capture regulated data that cannot be safely handled.

tradeoffs.benefit: Incidents are diagnosed faster because a request can be traced end to end.
tradeoffs.cost: Telemetry storage and processing add ongoing cost and capacity planning.

tradeoffs.benefit: Symptom-based alerts reduce noise and focus responders on user impact.
tradeoffs.cost: Good instrumentation must be designed into code, which lengthens initial development.

quality_impacts.note: Symptom-based alerts catch degradation early and protect the availability percentage before users report it.
Traces and dashboards shorten mean time to diagnose, keeping incident recovery within the RTO.
Logs and traces expand the data surface and can leak secrets unless fields are scrubbed deliberately.

items.mechanism: Attach a correlation identifier to each request, emit structured logs, dimensional metrics, and distributed traces, then alert on symptom-based service level indicators with runbook links.
failure_modes: Logging sensitive data such as tokens or personal information.
Metrics with unbounded label cardinality that overwhelm the monitoring backend.
Alerting on internal causes rather than user-visible symptoms.
Missing correlation identifiers so a request cannot be followed across services.

items.title: Queue-Based Load Leveling
items.summary: Place a durable queue between producers and workers so bursts are buffered and consumers process work at a steady, controlled rate.
items.decision: Accept work into a bounded durable queue and let workers drain it at a sustainable pace, exposing backlog depth as a first-class operational signal.
use_when: Incoming traffic is bursty but the backend has a steady capacity.
Work can be processed asynchronously with eventual completion.
Backlog depth can be monitored and acted on.
avoid_when: The caller needs an immediate result before returning.
Messages cannot tolerate any delay or reordering.
There is no plan for overflow or poison messages.

tradeoffs.benefit: Producers stay responsive and available during bursts instead of overload failing calls.
tradeoffs.cost: Completion is delayed and users need a way to observe pending work.

tradeoffs.benefit: Workers can scale on backlog depth with predictable throughput.
tradeoffs.cost: A queue adds delivery, deduplication, and dead-letter operational burden.

quality_impacts.note: Buffering bursts prevents overload from rejecting requests, sustaining availability during spikes.
Workers run near optimal concurrency so p95 latency stays stable rather than spiking under burst load.
Durable queued messages survive worker restarts, allowing replay within the RTO after a crash.

items.mechanism: Producers enqueue messages with a delivery guarantee, workers pull at a configured concurrency, and backlog depth drives autoscaling, throttling, or load shedding.
failure_modes: An unbounded queue that grows until storage or memory is exhausted.
Workers faster at enqueueing than processing, so backlog never drains.
No dead-letter path for messages that repeatedly fail.
Ignoring backlog age while watching only queue length.

items.title: Retry with Backoff
items.summary: Repeat a failed transient operation after a delay that grows between attempts, often with jitter, so a struggling dependency is not overwhelmed.
items.decision: Retry only failures that are likely transient, cap the attempt count, and use exponential delay with jitter to avoid synchronized retry storms.
use_when: Failures are transient, such as timeouts or brief network resets.
The operation is safe to repeat or is idempotent.
The caller can wait within an overall deadline.
avoid_when: The error is deterministic and repeating it cannot succeed.
The operation has non-idempotent side effects without a deduplication key.
The dependency is down for an extended outage and a breaker should open instead.

tradeoffs.benefit: Brief transient faults are hidden from users without operator action.
tradeoffs.cost: Retries add tail latency and can multiply request volume on a sick dependency.

tradeoffs.benefit: Jitter spreads retries so recovery is not delayed by a thundering herd.
tradeoffs.cost: More attempts consume worker capacity and can exhaust connection pools.

quality_impacts.note: Recovering from transient faults keeps request success above the target availability percentage during short disturbances.
Automatic repeat attempts let the system heal from brief dependency loss without manual intervention.
Backoff delays increase p95 latency when attempts are exhausted under sustained failure.

items.mechanism: On a transient error, wait for a delay that doubles per attempt up to a cap, add random jitter, and stop after a fixed maximum or a deadline.
failure_modes: Retrying permanent errors such as validation failures or authorization denials.
Retry storms when many clients back off in lockstep without jitter.
Amplifying load on an already degraded dependency until it fails completely.
Exceeding the caller deadline so the result arrives after the user gave up.

items.title: Saga
items.summary: Manage a long-running multi-service transaction as a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions that undo completed steps on failure.
items.decision: Replace a distributed transaction with an orchestrated or choreographed saga where each step commits locally and publishes the event that triggers the next step or a compensation.
use_when: A business process spans several services with separate databases.
The process is long-running and cannot hold a distributed lock.
Each step has a meaningful compensating action.
avoid_when: All steps can share one database transaction.
No reliable compensation exists for a committed step.
The process is short and a simple synchronous call suffices.

tradeoffs.benefit: Cross-service consistency is achieved without a two-phase commit.
tradeoffs.cost: Intermediate states are visible to other observers until the saga finishes.

tradeoffs.benefit: Each service keeps private data and independent deployment.
tradeoffs.cost: Every step needs a tested compensation, roughly doubling logic and test cases.

quality_impacts.note: Compensations return the system to a consistent state after a failed step, limiting data repair within the RTO.
Steps can be reordered or replaced in the saga definition without changing every service, shortening change lead time.
Each step and compensation pair needs failure-path tests, lengthening test runtime for the workflow.

items.mechanism: Define an ordered set of local transactions and matching compensations, track saga state, and on failure run compensations in reverse until the system returns to a consistent state.
failure_modes: A compensation that cannot fully undo a step with external side effects.
Missing compensation for a step that already committed.
Duplicate step execution after a retry without idempotent handlers.
Lost saga state that prevents knowing which compensations to run.

items.title: Arrays and 2D arrays: subarrays, sliding window, and in-place operations
items.summary: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory for O(1) indexing. Subarrays are contiguous ranges; sliding windows and prefix sums solve subarray problems in linear time. Two pointers on sorted arrays find pairs without nested loops. In-place operations on 2D arrays avoid allocating new matrices by using index algebra and element swaps.
concerns: O(n) or O(n^2) without O(n^3) brute force

claims.text: Sliding window processes each element at most twice, keeping subarray problems O(n) instead of O(n^2).
A prefix sum array answers any subarray-sum query in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing.
Two pointers on a sorted array reduce k-sum from O(n^k) brute force to O(n^(k-1)) by solving one subproblem in linear time.
Rotating a matrix 90 degrees in place uses O(1) extra space; allocating a new matrix uses O(n^2).
Computing product of array except self is possible without division by combining left and right products.

complexity.note: nested loop over start and end indices
cumulative total lookup

mechanics.heading: recursive structure: each subtree is a tree
mechanics.body: The key insight is that a subtree rooted at any node is itself a tree. This recursive structure makes induction natural. A function that solves the problem for a subtree can solve it for any tree by calling itself on the left and right children, then combining the results. Recursion eliminates explicit stack management for many tree problems.

mechanics.heading: search in a BST: left is smaller, right is larger
mechanics.body: A BST maintains the invariant: every node in the left subtree is smaller, every node in the right subtree is larger. This allows search to eliminate half the tree at each step, giving O(log n) search on a balanced tree. Insertion and deletion maintain the invariant by choosing a branch based on the comparison.

mechanics.heading: traversal orders: pre, in, post, level
mechanics.body: Pre-order visits the node before its children (node-left-right). In-order visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree (left-node-right); on a BST this yields sorted order. Post-order visits children before the node (left-right-node), useful for deletion. Level-order visits nodes by depth, layer by layer, and naturally uses a queue instead of recursion.

mechanics.heading: recursive vs. iterative traversal
mechanics.body: Recursion is elegant and matches the problem structure, but it uses stack space proportional to tree height. An iterative traversal uses an explicit stack (or deque for level-order) and avoids recursion limits. The choice depends on the tree depth and whether recursion clarity matters more than stack efficiency.

mechanics.heading: node-based structure: pointer chaining
mechanics.body: Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. Unlike arrays, there is no random access; reaching a node requires starting at the head and following pointers. mechanics.heading: reversal: redirect pointers in-place
mechanics.body: To reverse a linked list, redirect each node's pointer to point backward instead of forward. Iterate through the list, keeping track of the previous node. mechanics.heading: cycle detection: two pointers at different speeds
mechanics.body: If a list has a cycle, a fast pointer (advancing 2 steps per iteration) and a slow pointer (advancing 1 step) will eventually meet. If the fast pointer reaches null, there is no cycle. Once a cycle is found, the distance from the head to the cycle entry equals the distance from the meeting point back to the entry, a fact that allows finding the cycle start.

mechanics.body: Many linked list problems require tracking multiple pointers simultaneously: a dummy node simplifies edge cases at the head, a fast and slow pointer find the middle, or two pointers track positions in different lists. items.title: Bottom-up heapify is linear
items.summary: Constructing a binary heap by calling sift-down from the last internal node to the root takes O(n) time.
items.problem: Constructing a binary heap by calling sift-down from the last internal node to the root takes O(n) time.
items.statement: Constructing a binary heap by calling sift-down from the last internal node to the root takes O(n) time.
items.invariant: Before node i is processed, every subtree rooted at an index greater than i is already a valid heap.
items.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space, versus O(n log n) for repeated insertion.

steps.label: Leaves are heaps
steps.detail: Nodes with no children already satisfy the heap property, so processing can start at the last parent.

steps.label: Process internal nodes bottom-up
steps.detail: Walking from the last parent down to the root guarantees each child subtree is a heap before its parent is fixed.

steps.label: Cost depends on height
steps.detail: A node at height h moves at most h levels, and a binary heap has at most ceil(n / 2^(h+1)) nodes at height h.

steps.label: Bound the weighted sum
steps.detail: The sum over heights of h * n / 2^(h+1) is at most n, because the series sum h / 2^h converges to 2.

items.title: Dynamic array append is amortized O(1)
items.summary: A sequence of n appends to a geometrically growing array costs O(n) time in total.
items.problem: A sequence of n appends to a geometrically growing array costs O(n) time in total.
items.statement: A sequence of n appends to a geometrically growing array costs O(n) time in total.
items.invariant: After every append, capacity is at least length; immediately after a resize, capacity is at most twice length.
items.complexity: O(n) for n appends; O(1) amortized, O(n) worst case for a single resize.

steps.label: Base case
steps.detail: The first append writes one slot into the initial capacity and performs no copy.

steps.label: Resize points form a geometric series
steps.detail: Capacity doubles only when length reaches capacity, so resizes happen at lengths 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on.

steps.label: Total copy work is bounded
steps.detail: Across all resizes the array copies at most 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n slots, which is less than 2n.

steps.label: Add writes and copies
steps.detail: n appends perform n writes and fewer than 2n copies, so the sequence is linear and each append is O(1) on average.

items.title: Sliding window moves each pointer at most n times
items.summary: A sliding window over an array of n elements runs in O(n) time when each pointer only moves forward.
items.problem: A sliding window over an array of n elements runs in O(n) time when each pointer only moves forward.
items.statement: A sliding window over an array of n elements runs in O(n) time when each pointer only moves forward.
items.invariant: At the start of every iteration the half-open interval [left, right) is the current window and right is one past the last inspected element.

steps.label: Empty window
steps.detail: Set left = right = 0. The window is empty and the invariant holds before any input is consumed.

steps.label: Right pointer only advances
steps.detail: Each iteration admits at most one new element by increasing right, so right advances at most n times.

steps.label: Left pointer only advances
steps.detail: Invalid windows are repaired by increasing left; it never decreases, so left also advances at most n times.

steps.label: Sum the pointer moves
steps.detail: At most n expansions plus at most n shrink steps gives O(n) total work, with O(1) extra space.

mechanics.heading: Consumer-driven contracts: client defines expectations
mechanics.body: The client (consumer) defines what it expects from the server (provider) in a contract file. The contract specifies request format, response schema, status codes, and error messages. The provider implements to satisfy the contract; both sides validate against it.

mechanics.heading: Provider contracts: server defines its capabilities
mechanics.body: The provider defines what it guarantees: API version, supported methods, response schemas. The provider tests that it meets its contract. When a consumer violates the contract (e.g., sends invalid input), the provider's contract test might not catch it, but the consumer's contract test should.

mechanics.heading: Schema validation as a lightweight contract test
mechanics.body: Without a formal contract framework (like Pact), schema validation can enforce contracts: jsonschema, OpenAPI specs, or GraphQL schemas. Tests validate requests against schemas before sending and responses after receiving. This catches misalignment faster than end-to-end tests.

mechanics.heading: Contract tests in CI catch breaking changes early
mechanics.body: Contract tests run in CI before merging. If a PR changes the API in a breaking way, the contract test fails, preventing the merge. This is faster feedback than waiting for end-to-end tests or production issues.

mechanics.heading: Fixtures as dependency injection for tests
mechanics.body: A test declares its dependencies (database, mock service) as function parameters. Pytest matches parameters to fixture names and injects them. This decouples test code from setup logic and makes dependencies explicit in the test signature.

mechanics.heading: conftest.py defines shared fixtures
mechanics.body: conftest.py is a pytest convention file where fixtures are defined. Pytest discovers conftest.py files in the test directory and parent directories, automatically making fixtures available to all tests. This avoids importing fixtures explicitly.

mechanics.heading: Fixture scope controls setup reuse (function, module, session)
mechanics.body: A function-scoped fixture runs setup before each test and cleanup after. A module-scoped fixture runs setup once per module and cleans up after the module. Session-scoped fixtures run once per test session. Broader scopes reuse setup (faster) but risk test coupling; narrower scopes ensure isolation.

mechanics.heading: Fixtures compose: one fixture depends on another
mechanics.body: A fixture can take another fixture as a parameter. Pytest resolves the dependency chain and runs setup in order. This builds complex environments from simple pieces and avoids duplication.

items.title: Unit testing: test isolation, hermetic tests, and mocking strategies
items.summary: Unit tests verify single functions or classes in isolation, fast and deterministically. Hermetic tests are self-contained: they never touch external services, file systems, or databases. Mocking replaces dependencies, allowing tests to control inputs and verify behavior. Pytest markers (@pytest.mark.unit) organize tests by scope. Fixtures manage setup and teardown, keeping tests DRY.
concerns: O(1), verify exception type and message text

claims.text: Unit tests on isolated components run in milliseconds, not seconds, because they avoid I/O.
Hermetic tests mock all external dependencies: databases, networks, file systems, caches.

@pytest.mark.unit and @pytest.mark.integration allow running only a subset of tests before commit.
Mock external services (HTTP, database, file I/O); test real logic with real domain objects.

problems.title: Isolate a function from a database dependency
problems.pattern: dependency injection (pass mock as parameter or fixture)
problems.why: A function that queries a database cannot run fast or repeatably. Mock the database to return test data.

problems.title: Test error handling without triggering real errors
problems.pattern: mock.side_effect = ExceptionType() to trigger error paths
problems.why: Testing error paths without actually raising them lets tests run fast and verify both success and failure.

problems.title: Verify a function logs the correct message
problems.pattern: pass mock logger to function; assert mock.assert_called_with(...)
problems.why: Capturing logging without side effects; verify the function called log with the right args.

mechanics.heading: Isolation through dependency injection
mechanics.body: Tests pass dependencies explicitly: a function takes a database connector as a parameter, and the test passes a mock. This breaks coupling and makes behavior testable. Avoid global state; instead, inject or monkeypatch.

mechanics.heading: Hermetic tests: no external I/O
mechanics.body: Hermetic tests never hit the network, disk, or external services. All I/O is mocked or replaced with in-memory stubs. A test should pass or fail the same way in isolation, in parallel, or in a different order.

mechanics.heading: Mocking libraries: unittest.mock and pytest-mock
mechanics.body: Mock objects replace real dependencies. unittest.mock.MagicMock records calls and returns, pytest-mock wraps it. Mocks allow tests to verify behavior without running expensive operations (database commits, HTTP calls).

mechanics.heading: Markers partition tests by scope and runtime cost
mechanics.body: @pytest.mark.unit tags fast, isolated tests. @pytest.mark.integration tags cross-component tests. Markers allow running only unit tests before commit (@pytest -m unit), or integration tests in CI only.
